subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Does Tea Have Less Caffeine Than Coffee?
description: A 60-second lesson on Does Tea Have Less Caffeine Than Coffee?.

hook.text: People assume tea has less caffeine than coffee. Pound for pound, tea leaves actually contain MORE caffeine than coffee beans.

buildup.text: Dried tea leaves are about 3.5% caffeine by weight. Coffee beans are about 1.5%. Tea wins on concentration.

discovery.text: But you use far less tea per cup (2g) than coffee (10-15g). Less leaf per cup means less caffeine in the final drink.

twist.text: Tea also contains L-theanine, which moderates caffeine's effect. Tea drinkers feel alert but calm—not jittery like coffee.

climax.text: The 'tea has less caffeine' statement is true for the cup—but false for the leaf. Context determines the answer.

punchline.text: More caffeine in the leaf, less in the cup. Brewing ratio changes everything.

quiz.question: Why does a cup of tea have less caffeine than coffee despite tea leaves having more caffeine by weight?
options: Much less tea leaf (2g) is used per cup compared to coffee grounds (10-15g)

details.summary: Pound for pound, tea leaves actually contain more caffeine than coffee beans. However, far less tea is used per cup and steeping extracts less caffeine than hot water flowing through ground coffee. The result is that a cup of brewed tea has roughly half the caffeine of brewed coffee.
details.whyItMatters: This common myth reversal surprises most people and demonstrates that caffeine content depends on preparation, not just the raw plant material.
takeaways: Tea leaves contain more caffeine by weight than coffee beans
Less leaf is used per cup and steeping extracts less caffeine
A typical cup of tea has about half the caffeine of coffee

faq.question: If tea leaves have more caffeine, why does brewed tea have less?
faq.answer: A cup of tea uses only 2 grams of leaves steeped briefly, while coffee uses 10 to 15 grams of ground beans with near-complete extraction. The amount of plant material and extraction efficiency determine the final caffeine content in the cup.

faq.question: Can you increase the caffeine in tea to match coffee levels?
faq.answer: Yes, by steeping longer, using more leaves, or choosing high-caffeine varieties like matcha where you consume the entire leaf. However, over-steeping also increases bitterness, making flavor a limiting factor.
